# A worked outbreak scenario

*Generated by `npm run surge:example`. Do not edit by hand.*

**Vector-borne (malaria, dengue, chikungunya), caseload ×2 for 14 days, in Purnia, Bihar.**

Only the medicines that treat it are re-scored or moved: Artesunate + Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (ACT), Artesunate, Chloroquine Phosphate, Primaquine, Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, Paracetamol. A dengue outbreak does not raise demand for
oxytocin, and restricting the scenario to the pattern's formulary is also what keeps it inside four
seconds — this run took 463 ms.

| | Before | Under the outbreak |
|---|---|---|
| Critical positions | 16 | 25 (9 newly) |
| Expected shortfall, units | 6,371 | 17,322 |

## The part that is a policy question, not a modelling one

Raising demand alone produces a wall of refusals. That is the measured behaviour of this planner under
load: an outbreak raises both sides of the benefit/cost ratio, so the gate barely moves. What changes the
answer is the price of a stock-out — a ministry dial, exposed rather than baked in.

| | Routine | Emergency |
|---|---|---|
| One averted Vital unit is worth | ₹25 | ₹100 |
| Surge needs served | 14 of 76 | 35 of 76 |
| Refused on benefit/cost | 60 | 31 |
| Transport | ₹10,920 | ₹42,826 |

**14 of 76 surge needs servable at routine valuation, 35 at emergency, for ₹31,906 more transport.**

Both plans are returned, always. A scenario that reported only the emergency one would be presenting a
policy decision as a computation.
